'''Language equations''' are mathematical statements that resemble [[equation|numerical equations]], but the variables assume values of [[formal languages]] rather than numbers. Instead of arithmetic operations in numerical equations, the variables are joined by language operations. Among the most common operations on two languages ''A'' and ''B'' are the [[set union]] ''A'' ∪ ''B'', the [[set intersection]] ''A'' ∩ ''B'', and the [[Concatenation#Concatenation of sets of strings|concatenation]] ''A''⋅''B''. Finally, as an operation taking a single [[operand]], the set ''A''<sup>*</sup> denotes the [[Kleene star]] of the language ''A''. Therefore, language equations can be used to represent [[formal grammar]]s, since the languages generated by the grammar must be the solution of a system of language equations.

==Language equations and context-free grammars==

[[Seymour Ginsburg|Ginsburg]] and [[Henry Gordon Rice|Rice]]<ref name="GinsburgRice1962">{{cite journal|last1=Ginsburg|first1=Seymour|last2=Rice|first2=H. Gordon|title=Two Families of Languages Related to ALGOL|journal=Journal of the ACM|volume=9|issue=3|year=1962|pages=350–371|issn=0004-5411|doi=10.1145/321127.321132|s2cid=16718187|doi-access=free}}</ref>
gave an alternative definition of [[context-free grammar]]s by language equations. To every context-free grammar <math>G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)</math>, is associated a system of equations in variables <math>V</math>. Each variable <math>X \in V</math> is an unknown language over <math>\Sigma</math> and is defined by the equation <math>X=\alpha_1 \cup \ldots \cup \alpha_m</math> where <math>X \to \alpha_1</math>, ..., <math>X \to \alpha_m</math> are all productions for <math>X</math>. Ginsburg and Rice used a [[fixed-point iteration]] argument to show that a solution always exists, and proved that {{clarify span|the assignment <math>X=L_G(X)</math> is the ''least solution'' to this system,|reason=Indicate what 'L_G(X)' means, in particular, whether it is an expression in the grammar world or in the equations world. I guess, G+R showed that the least solution to the equation system coincides with L(G) in the grammar world.|date=October 2019}} i.e. any other solution must be a {{clarify span|subset|reason=Should probably be 'superset'?|date=October 2019}} of this one.

For example, the grammar 
<math>S \to a S c \mid b \mid S</math>
corresponds to the equation system
<math>S = ( \{ a \} \cdot S \cdot \{ c \} ) \cup \{ b \} \cup S</math>
which has as solution every superset of <math>\{ a^n b c^n \mid n \in \mathcal{N} \}</math>.

Language equations with added intersection analogously correspond to [[conjunctive grammars]].{{citation needed|date=October 2019}}

==Language equations and finite automata==

[[Janusz Brzozowski (computer scientist)|Brzozowski]] and Leiss<ref name="BrzozowskiLeiss1980">{{cite journal|last1=Brzozowski|first1=J.A.|last2=Leiss|first2=E.|title=On equations for regular languages, finite automata, and sequential networks|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=10|issue=1|year=1980|pages=19–35|issn=0304-3975|doi=10.1016/0304-3975(80)90069-9|doi-access=free}}</ref> studied ''left language equations'' where every concatenation is with a singleton constant language on the left, e.g. <math>\{a\} \cdot X</math> with variable <math>X</math>, but not <math>X \cdot Y</math> nor <math>X \cdot \{a\}</math>. Each equation is of the form <math>X_i=F(X_1, ..., X_k)</math> with one variable on the right-hand side. Every [[nondeterministic finite automaton]] has such corresponding equation using left-concatenation and union, see Fig. 1. If intersection operation is allowed, equations correspond to [[alternating finite automaton|alternating finite automata]].

[[File:DFAexample.svg|thumb|Fig. 1: A [[finite automaton]] with associated system of equations <math>S_1 = 1 \cdot S_1 \cup 0 \cdot S_2 \cup \{\epsilon\}</math>, <math>S_2 = 1 \cdot S_2 \cup 0 \cdot S_1</math> where <math>\epsilon</math> is the empty word.<ref name="BrzozowskiLeiss1980"/>{{rp|21}}]]

[[Franz Baader|Baader]] and Narendran<ref name="BaaderNarendran2001">{{cite journal|last1=Baader|first1=Franz|last2=Narendran|first2=Paliath|title=Unification of Concept Terms in Description Logics|journal=Journal of Symbolic Computation|volume=31|issue=3|year=2001|pages=277–305|issn=0747-7171|doi=10.1006/jsco.2000.0426|doi-access=free}}</ref> studied equations <math>F(X_1, \ldots, X_k)=G(X_1, \ldots, X_k)</math> using left-concatenation and union and proved that their satisfiability problem is [[EXPTIME-complete]].

==Conway's problem==

[[John Horton Conway|Conway]]<ref>{{cite book | last1=Conway | first1=John Horton | title=Regular Algebra and Finite Machines | publisher=Chapman and Hall | isbn=978-0-486-48583-6 | year=1971}}</ref> proposed the following problem: given a constant finite language <math>L</math>, is the greatest solution of the equation <math>LX=XL</math> always regular? This problem was studied by [[Juhani Karhumäki|Karhumäki]] and Petre<ref name="KarhumäkiPetre2002a">{{cite journal|last1=Karhumäki|first1=Juhani|last2=Petre|first2=Ion|title=Conway's problem for three-word sets|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=289|issue=1|year=2002|pages=705–725|issn=0304-3975|doi=10.1016/S0304-3975(01)00389-9|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="KarhumäkiPetre2002b">{{cite book|last1=Karhumäki|first1=Juhani|last2=Petre|first2=Ion|title=The Branching Point Approach to Conway's Problem|volume=2300|year=2002|pages=69–76|issn=0302-9743|doi=10.1007/3-540-45711-9_5|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|isbn=978-3-540-43190-9}}</ref> who gave an affirmative answer in a special case. A strongly negative answer to Conway's problem was given by [[Michal Kunc|Kunc]]<ref name="Kunc2007">{{cite journal|last1=Kunc|first1=Michal|title=The Power of Commuting with Finite Sets of Words|journal=Theory of Computing Systems|volume=40|issue=4|year=2007|pages=521–551|issn=1432-4350|doi=10.1007/s00224-006-1321-z|s2cid=13406797}}</ref> who constructed a finite language <math>L</math> such that the greatest solution of this equation is not recursively enumerable.

Kunc<ref name="Kunc2005">{{cite journal|last1=Kunc|first1=Michal|title=Regular solutions of language inequalities and well quasi-orders|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=348|issue=2–3|year=2005|pages=277–293|issn=0304-3975|doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2005.09.018|doi-access=free}}</ref> also proved that the greatest solution of inequality <math>LX \subseteq XL</math> is always regular.

==Language equations with Boolean operations==

Language equations with concatenation and Boolean operations were first studied by [[Rohit Parikh|Parikh]], [[Ashok K. Chandra|Chandra]], [[Joseph Halpern|Halpern]] and [[Albert R. Meyer|Meyer]]
<ref name="ParikhChandra1985">{{cite journal|last1=Parikh|first1=Rohit|last2=Chandra|first2=Ashok|last3=Halpern|first3=Joe|last4=Meyer|first4=Albert|title=Equations between Regular Terms and an Application to Process Logic|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|volume=14|issue=4|year=1985|pages=935–942|issn=0097-5397|doi=10.1137/0214066}}</ref> who proved that the satisfiability problem for a given equation is undecidable, and that if a system of language equations has a unique solution, then that solution is recursive. Later, Okhotin<ref name="Okhotin2010">{{cite journal|last1=Okhotin|first1=Alexander|title=Decision problems for language equations|journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences|volume=76|issue=3–4|year=2010|pages=251–266|issn=0022-0000|doi=10.1016/j.jcss.2009.08.002|doi-access=free}}</ref> proved that the unsatisfiability problem is [[RE-complete]] and that every recursive language is a unique solution of some equation.

==Language equations over a unary alphabet==

For a one-letter alphabet, Leiss<ref name="Leiss1994">{{cite journal|last1=Leiss|first1=E.L.|title=Unrestricted complementation in language equations over a one-letter alphabet|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=132|issue=1–2|year=1994|pages=71–84|issn=0304-3975|doi=10.1016/0304-3975(94)90227-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> discovered the first language equation with a nonregular solution, using complementation and concatenation operations. Later, Jeż<ref name="Jeż2008">{{cite journal|last1=Jeż|first1=Artur|title=Conjunctive grammars generate non-regular unary languages|journal=International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science|volume=19|issue=3|year=2008|pages=597–615|issn=0129-0541|doi=10.1142/S012905410800584X}}</ref> showed that non-regular unary languages can be defined by language equations with union, intersection and concatenation, equivalent to [[conjunctive grammar]]s. By this method Jeż and Okhotin<ref name="JeżOkhotin2014">{{cite journal|last1=Jeż|first1=Artur|last2=Okhotin|first2=Alexander|title=Computational completeness of equations over sets of natural numbers|journal=Information and Computation|volume=237|year=2014|pages=56–94|issn=0890-5401|doi=10.1016/j.ic.2014.05.001|citeseerx=10.1.1.395.2250}}</ref> proved that every recursive unary language is a unique solution of some equation.
